note: Ingredient-level evidence is not automatically finished-product evidence. Product dose, formulation, population, and outcome matching are assessed separately.

creatine-monohydrate.name: Creatine monohydrate
creatine-monohydrate.posture: Strong evidence for specific sports-performance outcomes; product-level directness depends on dose.
creatine-monohydrate.summary: Numerous human trials support creatine monohydrate for strength, power, training capacity, and repeated high-intensity activity. Evidence is much weaker for endurance performance.
creatine-monohydrate.studied_context: Common adult research protocols use an optional loading phase followed by about 3–5 g/day, or several weeks of lower daily dosing without loading.
creatine-monohydrate.safety: NIH ODS reports few safety concerns at typical studied doses in healthy adults; water-related weight gain is common. Individual medical circumstances can change risk.
creatine-monohydrate.product_directness: PERFORMANCE+ lists creatine monohydrate, but the current manufacturer page does not publish a creatine amount. The site therefore should not claim that the finished product delivers trial-equivalent dosing.

sources.title: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance — Health Professional Fact Sheet
The Effects of Creatine Supplementation on Upper- and Lower-Body Strength and Power: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

omega-3.name: Long-chain omega-3 fatty acids / fish oil
omega-3.posture: Established triglyceride-lowering effect at appropriate EPA/DHA doses; broader cardiovascular outcomes are context-dependent.
omega-3.summary: Long-chain omega-3 supplements can lower triglycerides. NIH ODS notes that high-dose prescription omega-3 therapy is used for elevated triglycerides, while evidence for other cardiovascular endpoints varies by population and dose.
omega-3.studied_context: Clinical effects depend heavily on actual EPA/DHA intake, not simply the presence of fish oil.
omega-3.safety: FDA and EFSA have considered combined EPA+DHA intakes up to about 5 g/day generally safe when used as recommended, though individual risks and medication interactions still matter.
omega-3.product_directness: V-OMEGA3 currently lists Wild Alaska salmon oil but does not publish EPA and DHA amounts on the manufacturer page. A triglyceride-lowering claim cannot be inferred from the ingredient list alone.

sources.title: Omega-3 Fatty Acids — Health Professional Fact Sheet
Association Between Omega-3 Fatty Acid Intake and Dyslipidemia: A Continuous Dose-Response Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
Dose-related meta-analysis for Omega-3 fatty acids supplementation on major adverse cardiovascular events

vitamin-d.name: Vitamin D
vitamin-d.posture: Established nutrient role in calcium/bone physiology and deficiency prevention; many broader supplementation claims remain unproven.
vitamin-d.summary: Vitamin D is required for calcium absorption and normal bone mineralization. NIH ODS notes that evidence for many non-bone outcomes is inadequate or contradictory, especially in vitamin-D-replete populations.
vitamin-d.studied_context: Clinical interpretation depends on baseline vitamin D status and dose. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the usual status marker.
vitamin-d.safety: Excess supplemental vitamin D can cause hypercalcemia and other serious toxicity. The adult tolerable upper intake level is generally 4,000 IU/day unless medically supervised.
vitamin-d.product_directness: Several current products list vitamin D3, but their manufacturer pages do not consistently provide dose amounts. Broad immune, metabolic, or performance claims should not be inferred solely from inclusion of vitamin D.

sources.title: Vitamin D — Health Professional Fact Sheet
Effect of Vitamin D Supplementation on Risk of Fractures and Falls According to Dosage and Interval: A Meta-Analysis
Effects of intermittent or single high-dose vitamin D supplementation on risk of falls and fractures: a systematic review and meta-analysis

magnesium.name: Magnesium
magnesium.posture: Essential nutrient with established physiological roles; supplement benefits depend on baseline status, outcome, form, and dose.
magnesium.summary: Magnesium is essential to many physiological processes. NIH ODS reviews evidence across blood pressure, diabetes, bone health, and migraine, but this does not support a single blanket therapeutic claim for all magnesium products.
magnesium.studied_context: Absorption differs by magnesium salt; citrate, chloride, lactate, and aspartate generally have higher bioavailability than oxide and sulfate.
magnesium.safety: Supplemental magnesium can cause gastrointestinal effects, and excessive amounts can be dangerous, especially with impaired kidney function.
magnesium.product_directness: Several products list magnesium or specific magnesium forms, but dose amounts are often absent. Form-specific cognitive claims, including for magnesium L-threonate, require separate direct evidence.

sources.title: Magnesium — Health Professional Fact Sheet
Magnesium Supplementation and Blood Pressure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials

probiotics.name: Probiotics
probiotics.posture: Evidence is strain- and indication-specific; generic probiotic claims are not scientifically interchangeable.
probiotics.summary: NIH ODS emphasizes that probiotic effects can be strain-specific. Some GI endpoints show modest benefits for particular strains or combinations, while other conditions have uncertain or negative evidence.
probiotics.studied_context: Species name alone is often insufficient; strain, dose, duration, population, and outcome matter.
probiotics.safety: Usually minor adverse effects in healthy people, but serious infections have been reported in severely ill or immunocompromised people. Special caution is warranted in high-risk populations.
probiotics.product_directness: SMARTBIOTICS KIDS lists named strains, which is more useful than a generic 'probiotic blend,' but product efficacy still requires matching those exact strains and doses to human studies. Other products list probiotics without full dose/CFU information.

sources.title: Probiotics — Health Professional Fact Sheet
Strain-Specificity and Disease-Specificity of Probiotic Efficacy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Strain-Specific Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis of Probiotics Efficacy in the Treatment of Irritable Bowel Syndrome

berberine.name: Berberine
berberine.posture: Supportive but heterogeneous evidence for glycemic and lipid outcomes in type 2 diabetes; weight-loss evidence is inconclusive.
berberine.summary: NCCIH reports some evidence that berberine may improve blood glucose, insulin resistance, and lipid measures in people with type 2 diabetes, but study quality, populations, formulations, and effects vary. Evidence for weight loss is not conclusive.
berberine.studied_context: Published studies use varied formulations and doses, often in people with diabetes or other metabolic disease. Results should not be generalized to all users or all products.
berberine.safety: Common adverse effects are gastrointestinal. Berberine can interact with medicines and should not be used during pregnancy or breastfeeding or given to infants.
berberine.product_directness: S-BALANCE and NOURISH+ list berberine, but current manufacturer pages do not establish a trial-equivalent berberine dose. Product-level glucose or weight-loss claims therefore remain unverified.

sources.title: Diabetes and Dietary Supplements: What You Need To Know
Berberine and Weight Loss: What You Need To Know
Glucose-lowering effect of berberine on type 2 diabetes

ashwagandha.name: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera)
ashwagandha.posture: Some evidence for stress and sleep, but preparation heterogeneity and study quality limit broad conclusions.
ashwagandha.summary: NCCIH states that some ashwagandha preparations may help stress and insomnia, while evidence for many other promoted uses remains insufficient. Meta-analyses report benefit for stress/anxiety and sleep but also substantial heterogeneity and limitations.
ashwagandha.studied_context: Trials use different root, leaf, and root/leaf extracts with different standardization and doses, so evidence is not interchangeable across preparations.
ashwagandha.safety: Short-term use may be tolerated, but long-term safety is unclear. Rare liver injury has been reported. NCCIH advises avoiding use in pregnancy and breastfeeding and notes several potential medication and thyroid/autoimmune concerns.
ashwagandha.product_directness: NOURISH+ lists ashwagandha but does not publish the extract type, standardization, or dose on the manufacturer page. Trial results cannot be directly assigned to the finished product.

sources.title: Ashwagandha: Usefulness and Safety
Effects of Ashwagandha on stress and anxiety
Effect of Ashwagandha extract on sleep

curcumin.name: Turmeric / curcumin
curcumin.posture: Promising evidence in some outcomes, including osteoarthritis, but formulations vary and authoritative reviews do not support blanket efficacy claims.
curcumin.summary: NCCIH says there is not enough evidence to definitively conclude that turmeric or curcumin is beneficial for any broad health purpose, though research in osteoarthritis and several other areas is active. Meta-analyses of osteoarthritis trials report symptom improvements in some settings.
curcumin.studied_context: Bioavailability varies greatly across curcumin formulations. Evidence from a standardized high-bioavailability extract should not be generalized to ordinary turmeric powder.
curcumin.safety: Conventional oral turmeric/curcumin appears generally tolerated short term, but gastrointestinal adverse effects occur. NCCIH warns that some highly bioavailable formulations have been linked to liver injury.
curcumin.product_directness: Multiple products list turmeric or curcumin-related ingredients, but dose and formulation details are often missing. Finished-product joint, anti-inflammatory, or metabolic claims remain unverified until those details match the studies.

sources.title: Turmeric: Usefulness and Safety
The efficacy of curcumin in relieving osteoarthritis

collagen-peptides.name: Oral collagen peptides
collagen-peptides.posture: Human evidence is mixed and outcome-specific; skin findings are sensitive to study quality/funding, while knee osteoarthritis meta-analysis suggests symptom benefit.
collagen-peptides.summary: Recent reviews of randomized trials report improvements in some skin and osteoarthritis outcomes, but skin evidence becomes much less convincing when analyses focus on higher-quality or non-industry-funded trials. Study products and collagen types vary.
collagen-peptides.studied_context: Hydrolyzed collagen products differ by source, peptide profile, dose, and co-ingredients. Finished-product claims require a match to the studied preparation and dose.
collagen-peptides.safety: Generally well tolerated in trials, but allergen/source issues matter, including fish and bovine sources.
collagen-peptides.product_directness: COLLAGEN COMPLEX contains both bovine and marine collagen plus multiple co-ingredients, but the manufacturer page does not publish a collagen dose. Existing trial results should be presented as ingredient-level evidence, not proof of product efficacy.

sources.title: Effects of Collagen Supplements on Skin Aging
Effect of collagen supplementation on knee osteoarthritis

glutathione.name: Oral glutathione
glutathione.posture: Bioavailability is formulation- and duration-dependent; biomarker changes are documented, but clinical health-outcome benefits remain uncertain.
glutathione.summary: Human studies have produced different findings. An older single-dose study found negligible systemic availability, while a 6-month randomized trial reported increased glutathione stores, and newer pharmacokinetic research suggests formulation-dependent absorption.
glutathione.studied_context: Dose, formulation, duration, and outcome matter. Raising a blood or tissue glutathione marker is not itself proof of a clinical benefit.
glutathione.safety: Short-term studies generally report tolerability, but the evidence base for long-term clinical outcomes and formulation-specific safety is limited.
glutathione.product_directness: V-GLUTATION lists glutathione but does not provide a dose or formulation specification on the current manufacturer page. Clinical benefit claims should remain under review.

sources.title: Randomized controlled trial of oral glutathione supplementation on body stores of glutathione
The systemic availability of oral glutathione
A Targeted Metabolomic Assessment of Oral Glutathione Bioavailability and Safety in Humans

caffeine.name: Caffeine
caffeine.posture: Good evidence for some endurance and high-intensity intermittent performance outcomes; effects vary by dose, habitual use, timing, and individual response.
caffeine.summary: NIH ODS notes that caffeine can reduce perceived fatigue and help sustain exercise intensity, with the clearest support for endurance and some intermittent high-intensity activities. It is not a universal strength or power enhancer.
caffeine.studied_context: Sports-performance guidance commonly discusses about 2–6 mg/kg taken before exercise. Lower amounts can work in some people, and higher doses generally increase adverse effects without reliably improving performance further.
caffeine.safety: Caffeine can cause insomnia, anxiety, jitteriness, gastrointestinal symptoms, and increased heart rate. Total intake from all sources matters, especially in products containing coffee, guarana, green tea, or yerba mate.
caffeine.product_directness: Several current products contain coffee or other caffeine sources, but manufacturer pages generally do not publish total caffeine content. Trial-equivalent performance or safety claims therefore cannot be assigned to those finished products.

sources.title: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance — Health Professional Fact Sheet
Wake up and smell the coffee: caffeine supplementation and exercise performance-an umbrella review of 21 published meta-analyses
Dose-Response Effect of Oral Caffeine Use on Aerobic Exercise Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

l-theanine.name: L-theanine
l-theanine.posture: Promising but not conclusive evidence for selected attention and cognitive outcomes; combination effects with caffeine are modest and context-specific.
l-theanine.summary: Recent randomized-trial meta-analyses suggest L-theanine may improve some reaction-time or attention outcomes, and theanine plus caffeine may produce small cognitive or mood benefits. Other cognitive measures are unchanged, and clinical significance remains uncertain.
l-theanine.studied_context: Recent meta-analytic findings include acute testing after single doses, often around 200 mg for L-theanine alone. Combination studies vary in both theanine and caffeine amounts.
l-theanine.safety: Short randomized trials generally report good tolerability, but the evidence base is much smaller than for established nutrients or caffeine and does not establish long-term safety across all populations.
l-theanine.product_directness: V NRGY lists L-theanine and caffeine sources but does not publish their amounts. The site should not claim that the finished product reproduces the doses or effects studied in L-theanine/caffeine trials.

sources.title: Cognitive and affective effects of L-Theanine: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 31 randomized trials
Effects of Tea or its Bioactive Compounds L-Theanine or L-Theanine plus Caffeine on Cognition, Sleep, and Mood

panax-ginseng.name: Panax ginseng (Asian ginseng)
panax-ginseng.posture: Small or context-specific fatigue and cognitive effects are possible, but pooled results are inconsistent and broad adaptogen or performance claims are not established.
panax-ginseng.summary: Systematic reviews report mixed results. Some analyses find small fatigue benefits in selected populations, while pooled overall fatigue and physical-performance outcomes are inconsistent. Cognitive findings are also outcome- and preparation-specific, so results should not be generalized across ginseng products.
panax-ginseng.studied_context: Ginseng preparations differ substantially in extraction method and ginsenoside content. Findings from one preparation should not be generalized to an unspecified ginseng extract.
panax-ginseng.safety: Short-term oral use appears generally tolerated for many adults, but insomnia is common. NCCIH notes possible drug interactions, blood-clotting concerns, blood-sugar effects, autoimmune concerns, and pregnancy cautions.
panax-ginseng.product_directness: V-LOVKAFE, V-NEUROKAFE, and V THERMOKAFE list Panax ginseng, but the current manufacturer pages do not publish extract standardization or dose. Trial findings cannot be assigned directly to these products.

sources.title: Asian Ginseng: Usefulness and Safety
Ginseng and Ginseng Herbal Formulas for Symptomatic Management of Fatigue: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Effects of Ginseng on Cognitive Function: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

l-arginine.name: L-arginine
l-arginine.posture: Mixed human evidence for selected aerobic and anaerobic performance outcomes; possible benefits are small or context-dependent and do not support broad performance claims.
l-arginine.summary: NIH ODS describes arginine performance findings as limited and conflicting. Newer meta-analyses report possible improvements in selected aerobic/anaerobic tests and VO2max, but effects vary by protocol and some pooled analyses show substantial heterogeneity. The evidence is not strong enough to treat arginine as a broadly reliable ergogenic aid.
l-arginine.studied_context: Clinical studies have commonly used about 2–20 g/day, often far above the amount that can be inferred from a multi-ingredient product with no disclosed dose.
l-arginine.safety: Short-term studies suggest up to about 9 g/day is generally tolerated, while higher doses more often cause gastrointestinal symptoms and can modestly lower blood pressure. Long-term high-dose safety is uncertain.
l-arginine.product_directness: V-NITRO lists L-arginine but does not publish its amount. A nitric-oxide, pump, strength, or performance benefit cannot be inferred from ingredient presence alone.

sources.title: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance — Arginine
Effects of Arginine Supplementation on Athletic Performance Based on Energy Metabolism: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
The effect of L-arginine supplementation on maximal oxygen uptake: A systematic review and meta-analysis

l-citrulline.name: L-citrulline / citrulline malate
l-citrulline.posture: Exercise-performance evidence is limited and conflicting; some acute resistance-exercise studies are positive, but overall support remains weak.
l-citrulline.summary: NIH ODS states that research does not provide strong support for citrulline or citrulline malate as an ergogenic aid. A systematic review/meta-analysis found mixed evidence for acute strength and power outcomes.
l-citrulline.studied_context: Many positive studies use citrulline malate rather than plain L-citrulline, sometimes around 8 g shortly before resistance exercise. These formulations are not interchangeable by name alone.
l-citrulline.safety: Short-term studies report relatively few problems, though gastrointestinal discomfort occurs. Long-term supplemental safety is not well established.
l-citrulline.product_directness: V-NITRO lists L-citrulline but does not publish its dose or a citrulline-malate formulation. The finished product should not inherit results from 8 g citrulline-malate trials.

sources.title: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance — Citrulline
Acute Effects of Citrulline Supplementation on High-Intensity Strength and Power Performance

glucosamine.name: Glucosamine
glucosamine.posture: Conflicting evidence for knee osteoarthritis symptoms; preparation-specific findings and guideline disagreement make broad claims inappropriate.
glucosamine.summary: Evidence is formulation-specific. A meta-analysis of oral glucosamine sulfate found a small-to-moderate reduction in osteoarthritis pain with little effect on joint-space narrowing, while authoritative guidance and other evidence remain inconsistent. Prescription crystalline glucosamine sulfate should not be treated as interchangeable with unspecified glucosamine products.
glucosamine.studied_context: Glucosamine sulfate, glucosamine hydrochloride, and pharmaceutical-grade preparations should not be treated as interchangeable. Dose and formulation are central to evidence interpretation.
glucosamine.safety: Large osteoarthritis trials have not identified major safety problems, but glucosamine may affect blood glucose in some people and may increase bleeding risk with warfarin.
glucosamine.product_directness: V-ITADOL lists glucosamine without a published form or dose. Its finished-product effect on osteoarthritis pain or joint function remains unverified.

sources.title: Glucosamine and Chondroitin for Osteoarthritis: What You Need To Know
Effects of Oral Glucosamine Sulfate on Osteoarthritis-Related Pain and Joint-Space Changes: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

msm.name: Methylsulfonylmethane (MSM)
msm.posture: Evidence is too limited to draw reliable conclusions for osteoarthritis or chronic pain.
msm.summary: The evidence base remains small. A meta-analysis including MSM/DMSO trials did not find a clinically meaningful reduction in osteoarthritis pain, and authoritative reviews continue to conclude that reliable efficacy conclusions cannot be drawn.
msm.studied_context: Small studies use different doses, durations, and combination products, making generalized efficacy claims unreliable.
msm.safety: The limited evidence base also limits confidence about uncommon adverse effects and long-term use, especially in multi-ingredient products.
msm.product_directness: V-ASCULAX, V-CURCUMAX, V-DAILY, V-ITADOL, and V-DAILY SACHET list MSM, but current manufacturer pages do not establish a study-matched MSM dose. Finished-product joint or pain claims remain unsupported.

sources.title: 7 Things To Know About Complementary Health Approaches for Osteoarthritis
Meta-analysis of the related nutritional supplements dimethyl sulfoxide and methylsulfonylmethane in the treatment of osteoarthritis of the knee

valerian.name: Valerian (Valeriana officinalis)
valerian.posture: Evidence for sleep problems is inconsistent; authoritative guidance does not support presenting valerian as an established insomnia treatment.
valerian.summary: A 2024 umbrella review found no convincing evidence that valerian treats insomnia, although some reviews report subjective sleep-quality improvement. Objective sleep outcomes, preparations, and study quality remain inconsistent.
valerian.studied_context: Short-term studies commonly use valerian root preparations at roughly 300–600 mg/day, but extracts and preparations vary.
valerian.safety: Short-term use appears generally tolerated in many adults, but long-term safety is unknown. Sedative effects, withdrawal after chronic use, and rare liver injury reports warrant caution.
valerian.product_directness: V-ITALAY lists valerian but does not publish a valerian dose or standardized extract. A sleep or insomnia efficacy claim cannot be assigned to the finished product.

sources.title: Valerian: Usefulness and Safety
Does valerian work for insomnia? An umbrella review of the evidence

echinacea.name: Echinacea
echinacea.posture: Possible small effect on cold incidence for some preparations; evidence for shortening or treating colds remains uncertain and product-specific.
echinacea.summary: The 2014 Cochrane review found that echinacea products had not been shown to provide clear treatment benefit for colds, though a weak preventive effect from some preparations remained possible. Species, plant parts, and extraction methods vary widely, limiting generalization across products.
echinacea.studied_context: Clinical trials use different Echinacea species and preparations. Without species, plant part, extract, and dose information, direct comparison to the research is weak.
echinacea.safety: Short-term use is likely safe for many adults, but gastrointestinal effects and allergic reactions can occur. Drug interactions are possible, and evidence in children, pregnancy, and breastfeeding is limited.
echinacea.product_directness: V-ITALBOOST lists echinacea but does not publish species, plant part, extract standardization, or dose. Finished-product cold or immune claims therefore remain unverified.

sources.title: Echinacea: Usefulness and Safety
Echinacea for preventing and treating the common cold

senna.name: Senna
senna.posture: Established stimulant-laxative activity with supportive constipation evidence; this does not support broad detox or weight-loss claims.
senna.summary: Senna is a stimulant laxative with human evidence supporting increased bowel movements and symptom improvement in constipation. That pharmacologic laxative effect is distinct from claims of systemic detoxification, fat loss, or generalized cleansing.
senna.studied_context: Senna products vary in sennoside content and dosing. Short-term constipation use is distinct from prolonged use or multi-herb detox regimens.
senna.safety: Senna is generally tolerated when used as recommended for short periods, but high doses or prolonged use can cause adverse effects and has been associated with clinically apparent liver injury.
senna.product_directness: V-TEDETOX contains senna leaf and senna extract, but the current manufacturer page does not publish sennoside content or dose. The site should not imply a predictable laxative effect or a detox benefit from ingredient presence alone.

sources.title: Senna
Efficacy and Safety of Over-the-Counter Therapies for Chronic Constipation: An Updated Systematic Review
Senna Versus Magnesium Oxide for the Treatment of Chronic Constipation: A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial

milk-thistle.name: Milk thistle (Silybum marianum)
milk-thistle.posture: Insufficient high-quality evidence for liver-disease benefits; broad liver-detox claims are not supported.
milk-thistle.summary: Systematic reviews of randomized trials have not shown reliable improvements in mortality, liver histology, or clinically meaningful liver-function outcomes. Evidence remains insufficient to support broad liver-treatment or detox claims.
milk-thistle.studied_context: Milk-thistle extracts differ in silymarin content and composition. Evidence from a standardized extract should not be generalized to unspecified milk-thistle powder.
milk-thistle.safety: Oral use is usually well tolerated, with digestive symptoms most common. Allergic reactions and supplement-quality problems can occur, and drug interactions are possible.
milk-thistle.product_directness: V-ORGANEX and V-TEDETOX list milk thistle, but the current manufacturer pages do not publish silymarin standardization or dose. Liver-support efficacy remains unverified.

sources.title: Milk Thistle: Usefulness and Safety
Milk thistle for the treatment of liver disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis
An updated systematic review with meta-analysis for the clinical evidence of silymarin

alpha-lipoic-acid.name: Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA)
alpha-lipoic-acid.posture: Some evidence for reducing sensory symptoms of diabetic peripheral neuropathy; evidence does not justify generic blood-sugar or weight-management claims.
alpha-lipoic-acid.summary: NCCIH notes that alpha-lipoic acid may reduce pain associated with diabetic neuropathy but has not been shown to be helpful for blood-sugar control. A 2023 meta-analysis of oral ALA found improvements in symptom scores but not several objective neurologic measures.
alpha-lipoic-acid.studied_context: Diabetic-neuropathy trials often use hundreds of milligrams per day, including 600–1,800 mg/day in oral studies. Outcomes and studied populations should not be generalized to healthy users.
alpha-lipoic-acid.safety: ALA can cause gastrointestinal or other adverse effects and may interact with glucose-lowering therapy. Evidence from clinical populations should be interpreted with medical context.
alpha-lipoic-acid.product_directness: NOURISH+, S-BALANCE, and VITALPRO list alpha-lipoic acid but do not publish a study-matched ALA dose. Finished-product neuropathy, glucose, or weight claims remain unverified.

sources.title: 5 Things To Know About Type 2 Diabetes and Dietary Supplements
Effects of Oral Alpha-Lipoic Acid Treatment on Diabetic Polyneuropathy

coenzyme-q10.name: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10)
coenzyme-q10.posture: Condition-specific evidence is mixed; recent meta-analyses suggest possible benefits in heart failure and statin-associated muscle symptoms, but certainty varies and broad energy or prevention claims are not established.
coenzyme-q10.summary: Recent meta-analyses report favorable outcomes for some heart-failure endpoints and a possible reduction in statin-associated muscle pain, while other reviews have found inconsistent or null effects. Evidence differs by condition, formulation, dose, and study quality, so CoQ10 should not be presented as a general cardiovascular or energy enhancer.
coenzyme-q10.studied_context: Clinical studies vary widely in dose, disease population, formulation, and treatment duration. CoQ10 presence in a multi-ingredient product is not enough to infer a studied clinical effect.
coenzyme-q10.safety: Serious adverse effects are uncommon in available data, but mild insomnia or digestive symptoms can occur. CoQ10 may interact with warfarin, insulin, and some cancer treatments.
coenzyme-q10.product_directness: NOURISH+, V-DAILY, VITALPRO, and V-DAILY SACHET list CoQ10 but do not publish a study-matched dose. Finished-product cardiovascular, energy, or statin-related claims remain unverified.

sources.title: Coenzyme Q10
Efficacy and safety of coenzyme Q10 in heart failure: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
Effects of coenzyme Q10 supplementation on myopathy in statin-treated patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis

resveratrol.name: Resveratrol
resveratrol.posture: Human evidence is heterogeneous and low-certainty for many cardiometabolic outcomes; anti-aging or longevity claims are not established.
resveratrol.summary: NCCIH summarizes low-certainty evidence suggesting resveratrol may influence fasting glucose or blood pressure in some people with type 2 diabetes, while other outcomes are neutral and more research is needed.
resveratrol.studied_context: Trials often use concentrated resveratrol doses far above typical dietary exposure. Dose, formulation, health status, and outcome strongly affect interpretation.
resveratrol.safety: Oral resveratrol appears generally tolerated in available studies, but it may interact with anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs and supplements.
resveratrol.product_directness: COLLAGEN COMPLEX and NOURISH+ list resveratrol but do not publish a trial-matched dose. Anti-aging, metabolic, or cardiovascular outcomes cannot be inferred from ingredient presence.

sources.title: Type 2 Diabetes and Dietary Supplements: What the Science Says — Resveratrol
Resveratrol bioavailability and toxicity in humans

zinc.name: Zinc
zinc.posture: Essential nutrient with established deficiency-related roles; cold benefits are formulation- and timing-specific rather than a generic property of zinc-containing supplements.
zinc.summary: Zinc is an essential nutrient. A 2024 Cochrane review found little or no effect on preventing colds but suggested zinc may shorten the duration of an ongoing cold, with more non-serious adverse events and substantial variation across formulations and study methods.
zinc.studied_context: Cold studies generally use zinc acetate or gluconate lozenges/syrups at substantially higher short-term intakes than typical multivitamin doses. Those results should not be generalized to ordinary oral powders or capsules.
zinc.safety: Excess zinc can cause nausea and other adverse effects and can interfere with copper status and some medications. Dose and duration matter.
zinc.product_directness: D-FENZ KIDS, NOURISH+, V-DAILY, and V-DAILY SACHET list zinc, but their use forms and amounts are not equivalent to studied cold lozenges. A cold-treatment claim would be inappropriate.

sources.title: Zinc — Health Professional Fact Sheet
Zinc for prevention and treatment of the common cold

vitamin-c.name: Vitamin C
vitamin-c.posture: Essential nutrient with established physiological roles; routine supplementation does not prevent colds in the general population, though it may modestly shorten them.
vitamin-c.summary: Vitamin C is an essential nutrient. Regular supplementation generally does not prevent colds in the general population, but systematic reviews find modest reductions in cold duration and, in some analyses, severity. Starting vitamin C only after symptoms begin has not shown consistent benefit.
vitamin-c.studied_context: Common-cold evidence often examines regular intake of at least 200 mg/day, with larger effects in people exposed to extreme physical stress or with marginal vitamin C status.
vitamin-c.safety: High oral doses can cause diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal cramps. The adult tolerable upper intake level is 2,000 mg/day, and high doses can worsen iron overload in people with hemochromatosis.
vitamin-c.product_directness: Several current products list vitamin C, but most do not publish a dose that can be matched to specific trials. Ingredient presence supports a nutrient-content statement, not a finished-product cold, immune, collagen, or antioxidant efficacy claim.

sources.title: Vitamin C — Health Professional Fact Sheet
Vitamin C for preventing and treating the common cold
Vitamin C reduces the severity of common colds: a meta-analysis
